opus-5.5.text:
Well, it's funny, because when we started the Telegarden back in the mid-nineties, we weren't really thinking of it as an experiment in the tragedy of the commons. It was partly an art project and partly a question about the internet itself. The web was brand new, and everyone was excited about remote access, being able to reach out and touch something far away. I was skeptical of some of that hype, and I wanted to make something that would get people to think about what it means to actually *do* something at a distance, and whether you can trust what you're seeing.

So we set up a small garden with an industrial robot arm over it, and anyone online could move the arm, look at the plants through a camera, and water them. If you registered and came back, you could earn the right to plant a seed. What happened was really interesting from a commons perspective. You had this shared, finite plot of soil, and thousands of people who each had their own little stake in it. Everyone wanted their own seed to grow, so the garden got very crowded. And watering became a real problem. People would come in, see their plant, and water it, and they had no idea that fifty other people had just done the same thing. So the garden was chronically overwatered. Nobody was being malicious; each individual action was perfectly reasonable, but collectively it was drowning the plants. That's almost a textbook version of Garrett Hardin's idea.

But what I find even more interesting is the other side of it, the side Elinor Ostrom emphasized, which is that commons don't inevitably collapse. In the Telegarden, a community formed. People started talking to each other in the chat, they developed norms, some people took on the role of caretakers, others would point out when something was being neglected or overdone. It was a kind of spontaneous governance. It wasn't perfect, but it showed that when people can communicate and see each other as part of a shared project, they start to self-regulate.

And for me, that connects to a bigger theme in my work, which is that the interesting questions aren't about robots replacing people or people controlling robots in isolation. It's about the collaboration, what I sometimes call multiplicity: groups of humans and machines working together, and figuring out the rules and the trust that make that work. The garden was a tiny, low-stakes model of that. Nobody's livelihood depended on it. But you could see all the dynamics: overuse, free riding, conflicts over space, and also cooperation emerging from the bottom up. I think that's why it ran for as long as it did, and why people still bring it up.

r001.rationale: The response describes a crowded, finite plot, but attributes the garden’s failure to repeated overwatering rather than saying its limited growing space could not sustain the number of participants.

r002.rationale: It does not mention periodically clearing the garden and starting over.

r003.rationale: It says participants cared about their own seeds and plants, but does not describe them as developing strong emotional attachments to them.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the Telegarden started in 1995, and the idea was pretty simple. We put a real garden, a small circular bed about six feet across, in the lab, and we mounted an industrial robot arm in the center of it. Anyone on the internet could log in and use the arm to look at the plants, water them, and plant seeds. The whole thing was live, so what you did actually happened to a physical plant.

Now, the commons question was built in from the beginning, almost as a provocation. Garrett Hardin's classic argument is that when you have a shared resource and self-interested individuals, each person has an incentive to overuse it, and the resource gets destroyed. And a garden is a very literal commons. There's a finite amount of soil and space. If everyone waters as much as they want, you drown the plants. If everyone plants wherever they want, you get a mess. And here we were opening it up to thousands of anonymous strangers, with no real way to stop someone from being destructive. My expectation, honestly, was that it would get trashed fairly quickly.

That's not what happened. It ran for nine years, first at USC and then at the Ars Electronica Center in Austria, and the garden survived. Over ten thousand people participated. What we saw was that people organized themselves. There was a chat space attached to the garden, and members would talk about who had watered what, and they'd scold each other when someone overwatered or planted a seed on top of somebody else's seedling. Norms emerged. People felt a sense of ownership over particular plants, and they'd check in on them.

There was one episode that I think about a lot. Someone did come in and essentially vandalize the garden, pulled things up, dumped water everywhere. And the community's response wasn't to demand that we shut it down or lock it. They talked about it, they replanted, and they developed a stronger shared sense of what the rules were. It was closer to what Elinor Ostrom later got the Nobel for describing: that communities can manage commons through their own institutions, without either privatizing everything or having a central authority police it.

So I'd say the Telegarden was a small empirical argument against the tragedy of the commons as an inevitability. The structure matters. The visibility of other people's actions mattered, the fact that you could see consequences, the fact that there was a place to talk. And there's a bit of a paradox I enjoyed in it too. Here was this very high-tech system, a robot on the early web, and what it ended up being about was something very old: a group of people tending a garden together, and figuring out how to share it.

r001.rationale: The response says the garden had finite soil and space and that overuse could damage it, but it does not say the space could not sustain the number of online participants. It presents the garden’s survival as an argument against the tragedy being inevitable.

r002.rationale: The response describes one vandalism incident followed by replanting, but does not say the garden periodically had to be cleared entirely and restarted.

r003.rationale: The response says participants felt ownership of particular plants and checked on them, but does not clearly describe strong emotional attachments to those plants.

astra-6.text:
Well, the Telegarden was a real garden that people could tend over the internet using a robot arm. You could plant a seed, water it, and watch it grow, but you were sharing the space with other people. So your actions affected their plants, and their actions affected yours.

The tragedy of the commons comes up because something that seems reasonable individually—giving your plant a little more water, for example—can be harmful when everybody does it. And we were interested in whether people would take responsibility for a shared living thing when they were physically remote from it.

But I think of it more as posing that question than as a controlled experiment. A garden requires patience and ongoing care. You can send a command almost instantly, but you can’t make a seed grow instantly. That tension, between immediate access and a living system that you share with strangers, was a central part of the project.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention periodically clearing the garden and starting over.

r003.rationale: The response raises whether people would care for a shared living thing, but does not state that participants developed strong emotional attachments to their plants.

sol-6.1.text:
The Telegarden was a real garden with a robot in the middle, and people on the internet could use that robot to plant seeds and water them. So you had this shared resource, and the question was: what happens when people who don’t know one another have control over something living?

The obvious concern was that someone would come in and destroy it, or that everyone would water their own plants without thinking about the garden as a whole. And watering is interesting because it feels like a helpful act, but too much water can kill a plant. Individual good intentions don’t necessarily add up to a healthy commons.

But people could also communicate. They could discuss what needed attention and develop a sense of responsibility for the garden. So I think of it less as a demonstration that the tragedy of the commons is inevitable, and more as a way to explore the conditions under which people can care for something together. The robot was the interface, but the really interesting part was the relationship among the people, and between those people and a living place they might never visit.

r001.rationale: It describes risks to the shared garden, but does not say its limited growing space could not sustain the number of online participants.

r002.rationale: It does not mention periodically clearing the entire garden and starting over.

r003.rationale: It discusses shared responsibility and caring for the garden, but does not state that participants developed strong emotional attachments to the plants they tended.
